philsol
=======
A fully vectorial finite-difference mode solver for optical waveguides in Python.

Why philsol?
------------
- Open-source and free, so every step of the calculation is inspectable and reproducible.
- A transparent alternative to closed-source, proprietary packages such as COMSOL Multiphysics for vectorial waveguide mode analysis.
- Useful when research transparency, customisation, or batch processing matters more than a graphical user interface.

What it does
------------
- Solves the 2-D vector Maxwell/Helmholtz equations for an arbitrary,
  anisotropic (diagonal permittivity tensor) refractive-index profile.
- Returns guided-mode propagation constants beta and transverse E-fields
  (Ex, Ey).
- Can reconstruct the remaining vector field components Ez, Hx, Hy, Hz.

Core algorithm
--------------
Direct implementation of:
  Zhaoming Zhu and Thomas G. Brown,
  "Full-vectorial finite-difference analysis of microstructured optical fibres",
  Opt. Express 10, 853-864 (2002).
  https://doi.org/10.1364/OE.10.000853

Time convention
---------------
e^{-i omega t}.  Propagation along +z is e^{+i beta z}.

Installation
------------
pip install philsol

Core workflow (three steps)
---------------------------
1. Build a refractive-index array n with shape (nx, ny, 3).  The last axis
   stores the diagonal tensor components [n_x, n_y, n_z].

2. Build the eigenproblem:
       P, matrices = philsol.core.eigen_build(k0, n, dx, dy,
                                              x_boundary=None,
                                              y_boundary=None)

3. Solve near a trial propagation constant:
       beta, Ex, Ey = philsol.solve.solve(P, beta_trial,
                                          E_trial=None, neigs=1)

Key functions
-------------
philsol.core.eigen_build(k0, n, dx, dy, x_boundary=None, y_boundary=None)
  -> P (scipy.sparse.csr_matrix), matrices (dict)
  Builds the sparse eigenproblem operator for the transverse electric field.
  k0 = 2*pi/lambda is the free-space wavenumber.
  n has shape (nx, ny, 3) and contains refractive-index values.
  dx, dy are the grid spacings.
  Set x_boundary='periodic' or y_boundary='periodic' for periodic BCs.

philsol.solve.solve(P, beta_trial, E_trial=None, neigs=1)
  -> beta, Ex, Ey
  Solves the sparse eigenproblem near beta_trial^2 using
  scipy.sparse.linalg.eigs.
  beta is the propagation constant; the effective index is neff = beta/k0.
  Ex and Ey have shape (neigs, nx*ny) in row-major flattened grid order.

philsol.construct.extra_feilds(k0, beta, Ex, Ey, matrices)
  -> Ez, Hx, Hy, Hz
  Reconstructs the remaining vector field components from the transverse
  E-fields.  Note that the function name retains the historic misspelling
  "extra_feilds".

philsol.classy.phil_class(n, k0, x_max=None, y_max=None, dx=None, dy=None)
  High-level wrapper around the solver.
  Methods:
    build_stuff(x_bound=None, y_bound=None, kx_bloch=0, ky_bloch=0,
                matrices=False)
    solve_stuff(neigs, beta_trial, extra_fields=False,
                poynting_vector=False)
    destroy_crap(fields=False)

Units and conventions
---------------------
- SI units (not Gaussian).
- Non-magnetic material: mu = mu_0.
- Relative permittivity tensor is diagonal:
      epsilon = diag(n_x^2, n_y^2, n_z^2).
- Grid flattening order is j*nx + i (y outer, x inner).

Limitations
-----------
- The code is not thoroughly tested; verify results against known solutions.
- SLEPc/PETSc solver is optional and can be fiddly to install.

Minimal example
---------------
import numpy as np
import philsol as ps

nx, ny = 120, 120
dx = dy = 0.05
lam = 1.55
k0 = 2 * np.pi / lam

n = np.ones((nx, ny, 3)) * 1.0
n[40:80, 40:80, :] = 1.45

P, _ = ps.eigen_build(k0, n, dx, dy)
beta, Ex, Ey = ps.solve.solve(P, k0 * 1.45, neigs=5)

# beta[i] is the propagation constant of mode i
# Ex[i] and Ey[i] are the flattened transverse E-fields

Citation
--------
Zhu & Brown, Opt. Express 10, 853-864 (2002).
Author: Phil Main <philmain28@gmail.com>
Repository: https://github.com/philmain28/philsol
